title: Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 13 Nov 2026]
Title:Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.

report.summary: A new audit finds abliteration is not uniformly harder on newer open-weight LLMs; success depends on model pair, method, prompt set, and KL budget.
report.background: Abliteration is a fine-tuning-free weight edit that removes refusal behavior from open-weight LLMs, typically by ablating a refusal direction. It matters because open weights let researchers and hobbyists modify safety behavior without retraining. The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimization-based variant, reported that direction-based abliteration increasingly fails on newer models. This paper tests that claim across five predecessor-successor release pairs: Qwen2.5 to Qwen3.8, Gemma-2 to Gemma 4, OLMo-2 to Olmo 3.1, Mistral Small 2409 to 3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B to Qwen3.5-4B. Using Heretic 2.0, several direction-based methods and ARA, the authors measure how many held-out harmful prompts remain refused under standardized prompts, search budgets, and KL-divergence caps. The question is whether newer LLMs are becoming systematically more resistant to refusal removal.
key_points: The study edited five release pairs in Heretic 2.0 using three or four direction-based methods—difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM, and J-space on the small pair—plus ARA. All runs used the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL-divergence cap, and selection rule. Removal difficulty was judged by WildGuard on 972 held-out harmful prompts from JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench, and a malicious-code bank.

Refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. After direction-based ablation, newer releases retained between -1 and +37 percentage points more refusal than predecessors; after ARA, the range was -26 to +34 points. Between-pair heterogeneity ranged from high to low depending on the scale and variance model, with I-squared values of 20% to 80%.

Method choice changed the verdict. ARA’s effectiveness loss relative to direction-based methods was smaller in Gemma and OLMo but larger in Qwen. Each ARA verdict rested on a single run, and some conclusions changed when the divergence budget or variance model changed. This makes single-method comparisons fragile.

Prompt source strongly affected conclusions. In Gemma, the apparent direction-based increase in refusal came from the author-compiled malicious-code bank and reversed on public prompt sets. Keyword counts at the tool’s window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by about 7 percentage points per model. Audits using one pair, method, or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions.

The central finding is conditional: whether a newer model resisted abliteration depended on the release pair, ablation method, and KL budget, not on model generation alone. Claims that safety is uniformly improving or that abliteration is uniformly getting harder are not supported by this multi-pair, multi-method audit.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this complicates safety narratives around open-weight releases. A model that looks more resistant under one abliteration method or prompt suite may not be under another, so safety evaluations should report multiple methods, prompt sources, budgets, and run-to-run variance. For developers, abliteration remains feasible but unpredictable: testing on the target model and prompt distribution matters more than assuming newer generations are harder. The KL-divergence budget can flip conclusions, so reproducibility requires publishing full configurations. For regular users, the practical takeaway is that refusal behavior in open-weight models is uneven and editable; safety depends heavily on which community edit, prompt set, and deployment context are used, not just on the base model’s generation.
report.tools: Follow Heretic 2.0 for direction-based ablation, ARA implementations for optimization-based refusal removal, and WildGuard as an automated refusal judge. The relevant evaluation suites are JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, and HarmBench. Watch for reproducibility scripts and model cards on Hugging Face, and test any abliterated model locally against multiple prompt sets and KL budgets before drawing safety conclusions.
